title: What Are Open-Ended Mutual Funds? Benefits, Risks, and How They Work
summary: What an open-ended mutual fund is, how it differs from close-ended and interval funds, when you can take money out, and what decides the tax.
body_markdown:
## What is an open-ended mutual fund?


An open-ended mutual fund is one that, in SEBI's words, "offers units for sale without specifying any duration for redemption". Put simply, it has no end date, and you deal with the fund itself.


A mutual fund is a pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager under SEBI rules. Your share is counted in units, each one an undivided share in the fund's assets. The NAV is the price of one unit.


Almost every fund you will meet is open-ended. Every type-of-scheme line in SEBI's category tables begins "An open ended...". SEBI names three structures in all: open-ended, close-ended and interval. See[SEBI's categories](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories) for the kinds of fund.


## How does an open-ended fund work day to day?


Each business day the fund works out its NAV, sells new units at that NAV and buys units back at NAV less any exit load. An exit load is a fee some funds charge if you sell within a set time after buying. Selling units back to the fund is called redemption. There is no entry load on any scheme.


The fund house divides the net assets of the scheme by the number of units outstanding. Most funds do this each business day. Liquid and overnight funds do it every calendar day.


Units follow from the NAV. At a made-up NAV of ₹24, ₹6,000 buys 250 units, before stamp duty.


Which day's NAV you get depends on the cut-off time. For most funds it is 3:00 pm on a business day. A business day excludes any day on which the money markets are closed. For a purchase, both your application and your money must reach the fund before the cut-off. Our[cut-off timings guide](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-cut-off-timings-all-you-need-to-know) has the detail.


Because the fund keeps selling and buying back units, it grows when people buy and shrinks when they redeem. The fund house confirms your allotment by email or SMS within 5 working days.


This open design also makes a[SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/systematic-investment-plan-sip) , investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, possible.


## How is a close-ended fund different?


A close-ended fund has a fixed term. You can buy only when it launches, and the fund does not buy units back before it matures. Maturity means the end date fixed in the scheme. Our[NFO article](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-an-nfo) covers how a launch works.


Open-ended Close-ended Interval


When you can buy On business days, at that day's NAV Only when the fund launches In set windows of at least 2 working days


When the fund buys units back On business days, at NAV less any exit load Not before maturity Only in those windows


End date None Fixed in the scheme None stated


### Can you sell a close-ended fund before it matures?


You can, but not to the fund. SEBI's rules say a scheme without daily investment and redemption must be listed on a recognised stock exchange. So a close-ended fund's units are listed. To get out early, you sell to another investor on the exchange.


You need a demat account. The price is whatever buyers bid. It can differ from the NAV, and buyers may be few.


Here is a made-up example. You put ₹30,000 into a close-ended fund at a launch price of ₹10, which buys 3,000 units. A year later the NAV is ₹11.20, so your units are worth ₹33,600 at NAV. If buyers on the exchange pay only ₹10.80 a unit, selling there brings ₹32,400. That is ₹1,200 less than the NAV value, before broker charges.


The same ₹33,600 in an open-ended fund is sold back to the fund at NAV. With a 1% exit load for the first 3 months, as one fund house's scheme document sets, selling within that time gives ₹33,600 × 0.99 = ₹33,264. After 3 months you get ₹33,600.


### What happens when a close-ended fund matures?


A close-ended scheme is wound up by redeeming its units on the date fixed in the scheme, unless it is rolled over. In a roll-over, unitholders get at least 30 calendar days to consent, and the units of those who do not are redeemed in full at the NAV on the maturity date.


SEBI's investor charter sets 3 working days for paying out the proceeds on maturity.


### What is a fixed maturity plan?


A fixed maturity plan, or FMP, is a close-ended debt fund with a fixed end date. Debt means loans to governments, banks or companies, held as bonds. AMFI's current list shows FMPs with terms in their names, running from months to years.


A fixed maturity is not a fixed return. No one promises an FMP's return. It depends on the bonds the fund buys and whether each issuer pays. SEBI bars fund houses and distributors from quoting an expected yield.


Close-ended debt passive funds must follow target maturity indices. A[target maturity fund](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/target-maturity-funds) also ends on a set date. What you get then is the value of the fund's bonds on that day, not a fixed amount promised in advance. For how a debt fund compares with a fixed deposit, see[debt funds vs FDs](https://koshex.com/blog/debt-mutual-funds-vs-fixed-deposits) .


### Are close-ended funds common today?


They are rare. In AMFI's NAV list on 30 September 2026, only about 50 close-ended and interval schemes published a current NAV. Most were FMPs and older tax-saving series.


Whether one suits you turns on the length of the term, whether you could live without the money until maturity, and how few buyers the exchange may show.


## What is an interval fund?


An interval fund lets you buy and sell units only in set windows, and between windows its listed units can only be sold on the exchange.


SEBI's rules for all interval schemes set four points:


- The units must be listed on a stock exchange.
- No redemption is allowed except during the specified transaction period (the window), which must be at least 2 working days.
- The gap between windows must be at least 15 calendar days.
- The fund may hold only securities that mature on or before the opening of the next window.


Very few exist. On 30 September 2026, AMFI's interval fund heading showed one scheme family with a current NAV.


## Can you always take money out of an open-ended fund?


On business days you can, at the applicable NAV less any exit load, and SEBI requires the money to reach you within 3 working days. If the fund is late, it owes you interest at 15% a year for the delay.


There are a few exceptions:


- **ELSS.** Units are locked in for three years from allotment. A lock-in is a period in which you cannot sell at all. See our[ELSS lock-in article](https://koshex.com/blog/your-elss-lock-in-period-is-over-whats-next) .
- **Life cycle funds.** SEBI sets an exit load of 3%, 2% and 1% in years 1, 2 and 3.
- **A systemic crisis.** A fund may restrict redemptions only for market-wide illiquidity, market failure, exchange closure or force majeure. A fund can use this for no more than 10 working days in any 90. It needs board and trustee approval, and SEBI must be told at once. Even then, anyone asking for ₹2 lakh or less is paid in full, and bigger requests get their first ₹2 lakh.
- **A segregated portfolio.** If a debt bond is downgraded below investment grade or defaults, the fund house may, with the trustees' approval, set up a segregated portfolio. Subscriptions and redemptions are suspended until it does, for at most 1 business day. See[what side-pocketing means](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-side-pocketing-what-does-it-mean) .


An exit load is not a lock-in. A lock-in stops a sale. An exit load is a fee for an early sale. SEBI caps an open-ended scheme's exit load at 3% of NAV. Each fund's scheme document sets its own. One charges 1% on units sold within 3 months of allotment and nothing after, and one equity fund's document says nil.


Same-day money comes only through the instant access facility, online, in overnight and liquid funds, up to ₹50,000 or 90% of the latest value, whichever is lower, per day per scheme. See our[liquid funds page](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/liquid-funds) .


A fund house can also stop or limit new investments, for example when it thinks the fund has grown too large. You can still sell your units.


For the steps to sell and the NAV you will get, see[how to sell mutual funds online](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-sell-mutual-funds-online-a-step-by-step-guide) .


## What are the risks of an open-ended fund?


The main risk is the fund's holdings, which move with the market. The open structure adds one more need: the fund must pay out redemptions, and SEBI's liquidity rules are built around that.


Market risk shows in the riskometer, the label SEBI makes every fund show, on six levels, checked every month. No one can promise you a fixed return from a fund.


Liquidity risk is the chance that a fund cannot sell a holding quickly at a fair price. SEBI has rules for it:


- All open-ended debt schemes except overnight, liquid, gilt and 10-year constant maturity gilt funds must hold at least 10% in liquid assets. Liquid funds must hold at least 20%.
- Open-ended debt schemes except overnight funds are stress-tested at least monthly for interest rate, credit, and liquidity and redemption risk. Only the trustees and SEBI see the results.
- Since February 2024, AMFI publishes monthly, for every mid cap and small cap fund, the days needed to sell 50% and 25% of the portfolio.


Costs also eat into what you keep. The expense ratio is the fund's yearly fee, as a share of your money, taken out of the fund's value.


One protection: if a fund changes what it fundamentally is, it must tell each unitholder in writing. You then get at least 30 calendar days to exit at the prevailing NAV with no exit load.


Koshex, as a distributor, talks you through sharp market falls before you redeem. More in[the risks in mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/what-are-risks-involved-in-mutual-funds) .


## How are open-ended funds taxed?


Being open-ended does not decide the tax. What the fund holds does. Under the Income-tax Act 2025 as amended:


- **Equity-oriented funds** (at least 65% in domestic listed equity shares, as an annual average): gains are taxed at 20% if you held the units 12 months or less. Gains of longer-held units are taxed at 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 in a tax year.
- **Specified Mutual Fund units** (more than 65% in debt and money market instruments) bought on or after 1 April 2023: gains are taxed at your slab rate, whatever the holding period. The slab rate is the rate for your total income.
- **Other funds' unlisted units:** the gain is long-term after 24 months and taxed at 12.5%. Held for a shorter time, it is taxed at your slab rate.


There is no TDS (tax deducted before the money reaches you) on a resident's redemption gains. For hybrid, international and fund-of-funds schemes, the class depends on what the fund holds during the year, so check the latest documents or ask a tax adviser.


A maturity payout is taxed like a sale. For Specified Mutual Fund units, the Act names gains "on the transfer or redemption or maturity" as short-term capital gains, whatever the holding period. Our articles on[how SIP returns are taxed](https://koshex.com/blog/how-sip-returns-are-taxed) and[tax on debt mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/tax-on-debt-mutual-funds) go through the rules with examples.
